title: Lior and the Portrait
premise: Folklorist August Voss arrives in the remote village of Lior's Hollow to record songs the locals refuse to sing twice, lodging in the house of Lior, a mute girl the village treats as both ward and warning. As August documents the songs, every mirror in the house begins reflecting one second late, revealing that the villagers' ritual of silence has been holding something at bay, and her recording of the forbidden seventh song invited it across. The entity feeds on memory, erasing August's past hour by hour while the village closes ranks to let it take her rather than admit what they did to Lior's mother decades ago. At dawn, August chooses to surrender her own memories into the mirrors—becoming the house's new reflection—to restore Lior's stolen voice and name, ending the haunting but leaving her remembered only by the girl she saved.
about_author: Marguerite Sterling is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories in disappearing rural communities before turning to horror. She writes about the violence of being forgotten and lives, deliberately, somewhere without mirrors.

chapters.title: The Songs They Won't Sing Twice
chapters.summary: August Voss arrives in Lior's Hollow with recording equipment and a scholar's detachment, interviewing villagers who answer politely but go silent when she asks them to repeat a single verse. She takes a room in the last house on the lane, belonging to Lior, a mute teenage girl the village seems collectively ashamed of. POV: August. Emotional beat: professional curiosity shadowed by the first prickle of being unwelcome.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Alone in the house at night, August notices her reflection in the hallway mirror lags—a blink arriving after her eyelid falls. She tests it scientifically, timing it, telling herself it's fatigue, while Lior watches from the stairs with an expression closer to pity than fear. POV: August. Emotional beat: rational denial beginning to crack.

chapters.title: What Lior Cannot Say
chapters.summary: August finds Lior's hidden drawings: the same woman's face repeated across years, always with the mouth scribbled out. When August gently asks about her, Lior presses August's hand flat against the cold parlor mirror—and beneath the glass, faintly, another hand presses back. POV: August, with Lior's silence as counterpoint. Emotional beat: tenderness curdling into dread.

chapters.title: The Seventh Song
chapters.summary: An old woman, Marta, finally agrees to sing for August—one verse only, of a lullaby no one will finish. That night August plays the recording back and hears a second voice underneath, harmonizing, singing words that make the mirrors ripple like water. Every reflection in the house now runs a full second behind. POV: August. Emotional beat: the thrill of discovery turning to guilt—she has documented something awake.

chapters.title: Village of Closed Doors
chapters.summary: August walks to the village seeking answers and finds shutters closing as she passes. The priest tells her the Voss family name isn't in any parish record, though she remembers her grandmother singing this region's tunes. Returning home, she can't recall her mother's face—only that she had one. POV: August. Emotional beat: isolation deepening as her own past begins dissolving.

chapters.title: The House Remembers Her
chapters.summary: Lior breaks her silence by writing: the thing in the mirrors was invited once before, by Lior's mother, to bring back Lior's dead father—and it took the mother's memories instead, then her voice, then her face, which now wears Lior's features in the glass. The village's twice-sung rule keeps it fed just enough to stay contained. POV: alternating August and Lior's written testimony. Emotional beat: grief and fury—the haunting is a cover-up.

chapters.title: Erasure
chapters.summary: August wakes unable to remember why she came to the village; her field notes are in handwriting that is becoming less hers by the hour. The entity speaks through the bathroom mirror in her own voice, offering to give everything back if she opens the front door before sunrise. Outside, the villagers stand in the lane, waiting, wanting her gone. POV: August. Emotional beat: terror of self-loss and the seduction of the bargain.

chapters.title: Justice Outside the Law
chapters.summary: August realizes the truth: the village let Lior's mother be consumed and named the child cursed to bury their sin. There is no law here, only complicity. She smashes every mirror except the great parlor glass, forcing the entity fully into one surface, and demands it return what it took from Lior—not mercy, but restitution. POV: August. Emotional beat: cold, righteous clarity replacing fear.

chapters.title: Sunrise Negotiation
chapters.summary: As the sky lightens, the entity offers a trade: Lior's voice and memories returned, but someone must take her place in the glass forever. August records one final entry—a confession naming every villager's silence—then steps toward the mirror before Lior can stop her. The first sunlight hits the glass. POV: August, then shifting outward. Emotional beat: sacrifice offered freely, the arc's emotional peak.

chapters.title: The Girl Who Sings Twice
chapters.summary: August's reflection remains in the parlor glass, calm and whole, while her body is found at dawn—or perhaps simply never found at all. Lior speaks her first word in nine years: August's name. The villagers, confronted by the recording, begin singing the seventh song openly, twice, as penance. In the mirror, sometimes, August smiles. POV: Lior. Emotional beat: sorrow braided with belonging—memory survives in the ones who carry it.
